title: Peace, Peace, When There Is No Peace
summary: The alarm sounds south of Jerusalem as an enemy prepares a siege, and God orders the ramp raised against a city full of oppression. Jeremiah complains that no one will listen; prophets and priests heal the people's wound lightly, crying peace when there is none. God invites the people to ask for the ancient paths and find rest, but they refuse. A cruel army comes from the north, and Jeremiah, appointed as an assayer of metal, finds the people to be rejected silver.
story: This chapter closes the first great cycle of Jeremiah's preaching (chapters 2 to 6), which moved from the charge of unfaithfulness, through the call to return, to the approach of the enemy from the north. Here the enemy is at the gates: tents pitched around the city, soldiers impatient to attack, a siege ramp going up. The chapter also introduces two themes that will stay with the book to the end: the false prophets who promise peace, and the prophet's own isolation as the only voice no one wants to hear. Chapter 7 then takes Jeremiah to the temple gate for his most famous sermon.
historical:
Like chapters 4 and 5, this chapter is undated poetry, usually placed in the period when Babylon's threat was taking shape, from the last years of Josiah into Jehoiakim's reign (roughly 609 to 598 BC), though it describes a siege like the one that came in 588 to 586 BC. The geography is precise. Benjamin was Jeremiah's own tribal territory, just north of Jerusalem; its people had fled into the capital for safety, and now they are told to flee out of it. Tekoa was a town about ten miles south of Jerusalem, the home of the prophet Amos, and Beth-haccherem was a hilltop between Jerusalem and Bethlehem, often identified with the site of Ramat Rahel. The alarm is raised to the south because the enemy is coming from the north, and escape lies southward.

Sheba (verse 20) was a kingdom in southern Arabia, famous for frankincense, which traveled north by caravan along the incense routes. The sweet cane from a distant land was an aromatic reed, probably imported from further east. Both were costly ingredients in temple worship.
cultural:
Ancient armies besieged walled cities by cutting trees to build ramps of earth and timber up to the walls, so that battering rams could reach the gates and upper defenses. Deuteronomy 20:19-20 forbade Israel to cut down fruit trees for siegeworks, but invaders had no such scruple. The soldiers of verses 4 and 5 want to attack at noon, then complain that the day is fading, then decide to attack by night; their eagerness adds to the terror.

Verses 27 to 30 draw on metalwork. Silver was refined by heating the ore with lead in a furnace, with bellows blowing air across it; the lead oxidized and carried off the impurities, leaving pure silver. Jeremiah is appointed as an assayer, testing the people like ore. But here the lead burns away and the dross remains, so the silver is rejected. The dressing of a wound in verse 14 pictures a healer who covers a deep injury with a light bandage, so that it festers underneath. Rolling in ashes and mourning as for an only son (verse 26) was the deepest grief a family could show, since an only son carried the family's name and future.
literary: The chapter is poetry with rapidly shifting voices: God commanding, the enemy soldiers speaking to one another (verses 4 and 5), Jeremiah complaining (verses 10 and 11), the people answering God with flat refusals (verses 16 and 17), and the people crying out in fear (verses 24 to 26). Two refusals in a row, We will not walk in it and We will not listen, are the hinge of the chapter. Verse 1 contains a pun that English cannot keep: the Hebrew for blow the horn (tiqu) echoes the name Tekoa. Verses 13 to 15 appear again, with small changes, in 8:10-12, a sign that the book gathers and reuses Jeremiah's sayings. The chapter ends with a verdict rather than a warning: rejected silver.

outline.t: Flee from Jerusalem: enemies ready to attack
Raise the siege ramp: a city of oppression
No one listens; prophets cry peace
A cruel army from the north
The prophet as assayer: rejected silver

doctrines.note: The chapter contrasts God's true word, which has become offensive to the people, with the prophets' soothing message of peace. God's word is meant to wound so it can heal; a message that only reassures leaves the wound to fester.
Stand at the crossroads and ask for the ancient paths: faithfulness means seeking the good way God already revealed, not inventing new ones. Walking in it brings rest for the soul.
God warns before he punishes, sets watchmen, and even tries to refine his people. Judgment comes when warning and refining have been refused, and it is the fruit of the people's own schemes.

words.note: Shalom, peace, wholeness, well-being, a life in which things are as they should be with God, neighbor, and land. The false prophets say Peace, peace when there is none (verse 14). They use God's richest word for blessing to cover up the fact that the people are far from it. True shalom cannot exist without justice and faithfulness.

Rapha, to heal, used for physicians and for God as healer (Exodus 15:26). In verse 14 the prophets and priests heal the wound of God's people lightly. They are false physicians who treat a mortal wound as a scratch. Jeremiah returns to this language often, and in 8:22 he asks whether there is no balm in Gilead.

Netivah, a path or track. In verse 16 the ancient paths are the tested ways of faithfulness that God revealed to Israel's ancestors. The word appears often in wisdom literature. The point is not that old is always better, but that the good way is not something the people must invent; it has already been given.

Bachan, to test or examine, used for assaying metals and for God testing hearts (Psalm 139:23). In verse 27 God makes Jeremiah a tester of his people, like an assayer. The test shows that they are not silver at all but base metal that the fire cannot purify.

christ: Jesus's invitation in Matthew 11:28-29, Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, closes with words that echo verse 16: you will find rest for your souls. Where Jeremiah told the people to find rest by walking in the ancient paths, Jesus offers that rest in himself, taking his yoke and learning from him. Jesus also stands in the line of prophets who refused to heal wounds lightly: he warned of Jerusalem's coming destruction and wept over the city because it did not know the things that make for peace (Luke 19:41-44). Jeremiah's lament over the false prophets' cheap peace prepares for the New Testament's claim that true peace with God comes through the costly work of Christ (Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:14).

hard.q: How can we tell a true word of peace from the false peace Jeremiah condemns?
hard.a:
The prophets Jeremiah opposed spoke in God's name and promised safety. On the surface their message sounded more like good news than his did, and many sincere people believed them. The book gives several tests. The false prophets' words did not address sin: they healed the wound lightly, reassuring people without calling them to change (verse 14; compare 23:17). Their lives did not match their message: they were greedy for gain and practiced deceit (verse 13). And their message fit what their hearers wanted (5:31). Deuteronomy 18:21-22 adds that a word that does not come to pass was not from God, a test that could only be applied in hindsight.

This does not mean every message of comfort is false. Jeremiah himself will announce peace and restoration in chapters 29 to 33. The difference is that true comfort comes after honest diagnosis and calls people back to God, while false peace denies there is anything wrong. Readers across Christian traditions agree that a message that never confronts sin is suspect, though they may differ on how to apply that test in particular cases.

questions: Where are you tempted to prefer a word that says peace, peace over one that tells you the truth about a wound?
What would it mean for you to stand at the crossroads and ask for the ancient paths? What old paths of faithfulness have you neglected?
Jeremiah felt alone and unheard. How do you respond when speaking the truth brings no visible result?
